We're building Fly Me To The Moon, turning NASA's Earth visualizations into dynamic sounds to make our planet's changing systems accessible in a whole new way. 

We're looking for creative minds in data science, research, and presentation to help bring Earth's story to life through sound
summary:
Earth Beats is an interactive website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It uses NASA-provided Earth science images and datasets to create audio experiences that allow users to explore our planet through sound.

The website presents existing scientific visualizations alongside their corresponding sonifications, transforming complex environmental data into an alternative sensory experience. This makes scientific information more accessible and engaging for people who may find traditional visual representations difficult to understand.

Our target audience includes people with dyslexia, children and students, teachers, museums, science centers, and anyone with a curious mind.

By combining visual and audio experiences, Earth Information Jukebox aims to make Earth science more inclusive, interactive, and enjoyable, helping more people connect with and understand the changes happening to our planet.

By translating visual patterns, colors, and data variations into audio, our project provides an alternative way to experience scientific information, making Earth science more inclusive, interactive, and enjoyable.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between visual data and sound, allowing more people to discover, understand, and connect with the changing world around them.
details:
Project Details – Earth Beats

How It Works

Earth Beats is an interactive website that transforms NASA-provided Earth science visualizations into sound experiences. Users can explore different scientific datasets, including nighttime lights, lightning activity, Japan and the Mediterranean at night, and fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions.

The website analyzes the colors, brightness, and intensity of different areas within the provided images. These characteristics are translated into sound variations, such as changes in pitch, frequency, and intensity. Users can move their cursor across the maps to explore different locations and hear the corresponding sounds. The website also provides an interactive 3D globe for exploring CO₂ emissions, alongside a flat-map view.

Additionally, users can access location information, understand what different colors represent through visual legends, adjust audio volume, and listen to on-screen descriptions through text-to-speech functionality.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project provides an alternative way to experience and understand complex scientific information. It makes Earth science more engaging and accessible, particularly for people with dyslexia, children and students, teachers, museums, science centers, and anyone interested in exploring our planet.

By combining visualizations with sound and spoken descriptions, the project encourages inclusive learning and allows users to experience scientific data through more than one sensory channel.

Tools and Technologies

We developed the project using several technologies:

  • Python: Used for backend development and processing scientific image data.
  • Flask: Used to build the backend, manage API endpoints, and connect the frontend with the data-processing functionality.
  • NumPy: Used to analyze pixel values, brightness, color balance, and data intensity.
  • Pillow (PIL): Used to load, resize, and process NASA-provided images.
  • HTML: Used to structure the website.
  • CSS: Used to design the interface and create its visual experience.
  • JavaScript: Used to handle user interactions, map exploration, and audio functionality.
  • Three.js: Used to create the interactive 3D globe.
  • Web Audio API: Used to generate dynamic sounds based on the analyzed data.
  • Web Speech API: Used to provide spoken descriptions of website content.
  • HTML Canvas: Used to render and interact with 2D scientific maps.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Earth Beats lies in transforming scientific visualizations into interactive audio experiences. Instead of simply displaying maps and graphs, we allow users to explore the information through sound that changes according to the underlying data.

Each dataset has its own sound characteristics. For example, nighttime light variations produce different tones, lightning intensity is represented through thunder-like sounds, and Mediterranean data is accompanied by wave-like audio. The project also combines 2D maps, an interactive 3D globe, color legends, and spoken descriptions to create a multi-sensory experience.

Factors Considered

During development, we focused on accessibility, simplicity, accuracy, and user experience. We considered how to represent different data characteristics through meaningful sounds while maintaining the connection between the original scientific information and its audio representation.

We also considered different audiences and levels of scientific knowledge, ensuring that the interface is easy to navigate and that users can explore the datasets without needing advanced scientific knowledge.

Ultimately, our goal is to make Earth science more inclusive and engaging by giving people a new way to explore, hear, and understand the information hidden within our planet's data.
